results.summary: This design implements a pseudo-random snake that moves across a 7-segment display. The user inputs a number via switches, which seeds the random movement, and the snake's position is shown on the display. It requires an external 7-segment display and switch inputs for operation. The documentation is minimal, providing only a basic description and test instructions.

This project implements a Tsetlin Machine, a binary classifier with on-chip training, using a 4-feature, 4-clause architecture. It uses pure digital logic and finite state machines instead of arithmetic multipliers, making it suitable for ultra-low-power Edge AI. The design includes 32 Tsetlin Automata, each implemented as a 4-bit saturating up/down counter. It is optimized for low-power operation and targets edge AI applications.

This design is a small UART-driven ALU processor. It receives commands and data via a UART interface and performs arithmetic and logic operations. The processor is controlled through the serial link, making it suitable for simple embedded tasks. The design is implemented in Chisel and includes a UART interface for communication.

This project is a demoscene-style visual effect for the Tiny Tapeout platform. It generates a graphical output that is displayed on a VGA monitor. The design is intended to showcase visual effects and is likely used for entertainment or demonstration. It requires a VGA display to view the output.

This project generates a cellular automaton pattern and displays it on a VGA monitor. The design uses a signal generator to produce the pattern, which is then rendered as graphics. It requires a VGA display to view the output. The documentation is sparse, but the design appears to be a visual demonstration of cellular automata.

This project is a simple VGA-based game where the user controls a box on the screen. The game uses a VGA output to display the graphics and likely accepts input from switches or buttons. The design is interactive and requires a VGA monitor to play. The documentation is minimal, but the game appears to be a basic interactive demonstration.

This project is a simple VGA GPU that uses an ALU pipeline to compute pixel colors based on the pixel's x/y coordinates and a few configurable registers. The design takes pixel coordinates as input and outputs a color, with parameters set via registers. The documentation is very sparse, with testing instructions only suggesting to read the Verilog code, indicating limited support for users.
